title: Factorising a Negative HCF

findings.finding: The introductory examples use numerical and algebraic HCF selection, signed division and cancellation of common variables without an opening review of these prerequisites.
findings.breakdown: Following −4x(−3+y) requires identifying 4x as the common factor and calculating 12x÷(−4x)=−3 and −4xy÷(−4x)=y. Gaps in these prerequisites can obscure how dividing by the negative factor determines the bracket terms.
findings.checked: The complete teaching contains no earlier topic or opening review. Both examples directly use these substantial prerequisites. p3-information states the factorisation procedure but does not rehearse them; guided practice follows the examples. The proposed review answers are correct and the items fit comfortably within one page.
findings.assumptions: HCF selection, signed integer division and cancellation of common variables are prior knowledge from the course’s algebra and integer topics. No calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: Before p3-information, add: ‘Find the positive HCF: (a) 8 and 16; (b) 12x and 4xy. Calculate: (c) −16÷−8; (d) 12÷−4; (e) −4÷−4. Simplify: (f) 12x÷4x; (g) 4xy÷4x.’ Answers: 8, 4x, 2, −3, 1, 3, y.

findings.doneWhen: Before the examples, students rehearse HCF selection, signed division and cancellation of common variables, allowing the teacher to address gaps.

findings.finding: Extend the paired factorisations by asking students to explain and generalise their sign relationship.
findings.breakdown: The task turns the two forms practised in p6-q7 into an explanation of why reversing both factors’ signs preserves the expression.
findings.checked: 2xy(−3x+5y−1)=−2xy(3x−5y+1). More generally, HB=(−H)(−B). The identity holds even when a factor is zero and requires only the sign and factorisation methods available by the end of the topic.
findings.assumptions: Students have completed p6-q7 and encountered positive and negative common-factor forms.

repair.proposal: After p6-q7, offer: ‘An expression has been factorised as −2xy(3x−5y+1). Without expanding, write it with outside factor +2xy and explain your changes. Generalise: if an expression is H times a bracket, what bracket is needed when the outside factor becomes −H?’ Expected answer: 2xy(−3x+5y−1). Every bracket term changes sign; changing both factors’ signs preserves their product. Generally, HB=(−H)(−B).

findings.doneWhen: The optional task asks for both the alternative factorisation and an explanation of the general sign relationship.
